title: Metzora: the bird set free (Leviticus 14:7)
hook: one bird is let go over the open field

segments.voice: Yesterday in Metzora, cedar and hyssop: the tall brought low. Your line was from cedar to hyssop. Did you let someone be right without adding a but? Today, the two birds in that bundle. Day four hundred two.

If you've ever opened a window to let a trapped bird out of a room, you know the moment. It panics against the glass, and then, all at once, it finds the gap and it's gone. Silence, and an open sky. Of everything in the ritual for coming home from tzara'at, the moment people tend to remember is a bird flying away. Outside the camp, the priest stands with the person who has been healed. Two small birds, alike. And only one of them will still be there at the end.
screen: `THE BIRD FINDS THE GAP.` → `TWO SMALL BIRDS, ALIKE.` → `ONLY ONE STAYS.`

segments.voice: First, why birds at all. Rashi offers an answer: the affliction came from chattering, from careless speech, so the person brings birds, which chirp and twitter all day. Their offering looks like the very thing that got them in trouble. Second, the two fates. One bird is slaughtered over an earthen bowl of fresh running water. The living bird is dipped, along with the cedar, scarlet and hyssop, and the person is sprinkled seven times. Then the priest lets the living bird go, in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation, "into the open field." Third, which way it flies. The Mishnah adds a detail: the bird isn't sent toward the sea, or toward a city, or into the desert. Toward the open field. Somewhere a bird can live. Fourth, what the free bird means. The Torah doesn't say, and readers have offered different answers. Some say the impurity is carried off and away. Many hear the person in the bird: someone who was shut outside, now released, flying back to life. And some teachers put the two birds side by side. The same kind of speech can wound, or it can sing. One bird is the old way of talking, ended. The other is the voice set free to start again. All of these are interpretations. What the text gives us is the picture itself: the priest's hands opening, and a small bird climbing over a field.
screen: `BIRDS, BECAUSE BIRDS CHATTER.` · `ONE OFFERED, ONE DIPPED.` · `TOWARD THE OPEN FIELD.` · `THE TEXT DOESN'T SAY WHY.` · then, large: `LET THE BIRD GO.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let one thing go. Settle, and breathe. Think of something you're holding onto that's done its time: an old resentment, a story you keep retelling about yourself, a hurt that's already been answered. Picture it as a small bird in your cupped hands. Feel how tightly you're holding. Then, on an out-breath, picture your hands opening, and the bird lifting toward an open field. You don't have to watch where it goes. The bell holds the time.
Metzora. The portion where, at the end of the healing rite, a living bird is set free over an open field.
Your line: let the bird go. Today, when an old grievance flies back into your head, open your hands, literally, and let it pass. Day four hundred two.

howItsDone: The bird ritual of Leviticus 14 belonged to the Temple era and is not performed today; Jews study it in the weekly Torah reading, and teachers often draw lessons about speech and release from it.

fork.setup: you're the priest, holding the living bird, dipped and ready. which way do you send it?
fork.reveal: toward the open field, the text says, and the Mishnah adds: not the sea, not a city, not the desert.

original.note: Hebrew: bird. two tziporim are brought for the healing rite in Leviticus 14.

trapdoor: what you thought: a strange animal ritual.
what it means: a picture of release: the one who was shut out is free to fly back to life.
what a scholar hears: Rashi on 14:4 links the birds to chatter; Mishnah Negaim 14:1 says the bird goes toward the field, not the sea, the city or the wilderness.

notes: JPS 1917 Lev 14:7 ends '...the living bird into the open field'; only 'into the open field' is quoted. Confirm.

Mishnah Negaim 14:1 on the direction of the bird (not toward sea, city or wilderness): cited from memory; the passage may be 14:2 in standard numbering. Note the Mishnah phrases it as the priest not turning his face toward sea, city or wilderness. Confirm.
The 'two kinds of speech' reading of the two birds is a common homiletic reading; attributed to 'some teachers'.
Rashi on 14:4: birds because afflictions come from chatter (pitputei devarim); confirm.
